result: The coupled dynamics of filament polymerization, motor attachment-detachment, and crosslink attachment-detachment induce spatial organization of motors and crosslinks along filaments. Crosslink depletion near filament plus ends results from the finite time required to decorate newly polymerized sections, while motor depletion arises from the time required to dress newly created filament overlaps.
evaluation: Claims C4, C21, C38, and C39 collectively establish the theoretical framework and mechanism for self-organization. The mathematical model (Equations 1-3) demonstrates how coupled dynamics lead to depletion zones with characteristic lengths |v_t - v_m|τ_m and v_tτ_c, providing quantitative support for the spatial organization mechanism.

result: Self-organization allows cytoskeletal bundles to generate extension instead of contraction and enables reversals of filament apparent velocities. Extension arises when motor run-length and unbinding rate are relatively large compared to filament length and crosslink unbinding rate, with the localization of motors and crosslinks near filament ends driving the switch between contraction and extension.
evaluation: Claims C5, C6, C17, C22, and C23 present the central theoretical predictions supported by analytical solutions (Equations 3-5) and phase diagrams (Figures 4-5). The transcendental equation (Equation 4) and stability analysis provide rigorous mathematical support for the existence of both contractile and extensile regimes, with clear parameter dependencies.

result: The extension mechanism differs from previously modeled behaviors in both cause and applicability. Unlike prior models requiring motor dwelling at filament ends or parallel filament interactions, the present mechanism operates through depletion-driven self-organization in antiparallel filament bundles.
evaluation: Claims C18 and C47-C53 distinguish the present mechanism from prior theoretical work through systematic comparison. The model explicitly excludes mechanical nonlinearities (C27) and position-dependent motor velocity (C28), and the comparison with Belmonte et al. (2017), Kruse and Sekimoto (2002), and Gao et al. (2015) is supported by appropriate citations.

result: Self-organization dominates over buckling-induced contraction in tightly connected actomyosin bundles where filament buckling is hampered. The tensions generated by self-organization exceed those from mechanical nonlinearities over broad parameter ranges, and the two mechanisms can operate simultaneously with additive contributions.
evaluation: Claims C24, C67, C68, C70, and C72 are supported by quantitative comparison in Figure 6. The analysis establishes bounds for buckling (ℓ₀⁻ and ℓ₀⁺) and demonstrates self-organization dominance outside the buckling-allowed region and even within it for certain parameter values. The assumption of additive contributions (C68) is physically justified.

result: Self-organization outcompetes motor dwelling in microtubule systems where filaments are long enough for end-dwelling to be rare. The self-organization mechanism contributes substantially to force generation not only when motors do not dwell, but also in many situations where they do.
evaluation: Claims C25, C73, and C79 are supported by the quantitative comparison in Figure 7 and the dwelling model analysis (Equations 7). The analysis shows self-organization dominates when extended depletion profiles develop (large τ_c or L) and when fast treadmilling prevents dwelling (v_t > 1), with appropriate experimental citations supporting motor dwelling observations.

result: The model predicts two experimentally observable transitions: contraction-to-extension and velocity reversal (plus-end-directed to minus-end-directed apparent filament motion). These transitions are detectable through direct imaging of bundles and single-filament tracking, and could serve as experimental signatures of self-organization-driven force generation.
evaluation: Claims C56, C57, C58, C83, and C84 identify testable predictions supported by the phase diagrams (Figures 4-5). The transitions are shown to be accessible by varying experimentally controllable parameters (L, v_t, τ_c, τ_m), with appropriate citations to experimental methods (Thoresen et al., 2011; Reymann et al., 2012; Murrell and Gardel, 2012).

result: The magnitude of forces and velocities predicted by the model are on par with those found in vivo, specifically in the cytokinetic ring of fission yeast.
evaluation: Claim C62 is supported by quantitative calculations showing contractile force ~120 pN (comparable to measured 390 pN) and velocity v_m⁰ ~ 5 nm·s⁻¹ (comparable to observed 3-4 nm·s⁻¹). The order-of-magnitude agreement validates the model's biological relevance, though the force prediction is somewhat lower than experimental values.

result: The predicted reversal from contraction to extension mirrors recent experimental observations in microtubule systems and actin bundles. Extension is observed in microtubules when polymerization/depolymerization dynamics is blocked in vitro, and both behaviors have been reported in stiff actin bundles.
evaluation: Claims C7, C19, C99, and C100 connect theoretical predictions to experimental observations through appropriate citations (Sanchez et al., 2012; Keber et al., 2014; Roostalu et al., 2018; Stam et al., 2017). The qualitative agreement between predictions and observations supports the model's relevance, though detailed quantitative validation would strengthen this result.

result: The qualitative predictions are robust to various simplifying assumptions. Extension is predicted whenever filament plus ends polymerize quickly enough to induce significant crosslink depletion, and this mechanism is insensitive to details of filament disassembly, crosslink unbinding kinetics, motor number fluctuations, and motor force-velocity relationships.
evaluation: Claims C85-C91 and C93 argue for robustness through physical reasoning about the underlying mechanisms. The arguments are logical and well-justified: depletion depends on time scales rather than specific molecular details, making the qualitative predictions robust. However, these are theoretical arguments rather than explicit demonstrations through sensitivity analysis.

result: The prediction of extension provides a stringent experimental test to validate or invalidate self-organization mechanisms. The absence of extension in certain parameter regimes (e.g., Thoresen et al. experiments with v_t = 0) argues against self-organization in favor of alternative mechanisms, while self-organization likely plays a role in vivo where buckling is not observed and treadmilling is crucial.
evaluation: Claims C94, C95, C97, and C98 provide a logical framework for interpreting experiments. The comparison with Thoresen et al. (2011, 2013) showing discrepancy with model predictions (extension predicted but contraction observed) appropriately suggests buckling dominates in that system, validating the discriminatory power of the predictions.

result: The model assumes rigid filaments, position-independent motor velocity, and neglects viscous drag. The insights from treadmilling dynamics are claimed to be applicable to microtubules despite their different mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C27, C28, C30, and C32 state explicit model assumptions. The rigidity assumption (C27) and position-independent velocity (C28) are justified as excluding alternative mechanisms. Neglecting viscous drag (C32) is retrospectively justified by showing drag forces (~7×10⁻¹⁸ N) are much smaller than motor forces. The applicability to microtubules (C30) is argued in the Discussion (C88-C89) with reasonable physical justification.

result: The analytical approach allows derivation of a complete phase diagram for self-organized motor-filament bundles, uncovering two previously unreported transitions.
evaluation: Claims C82 and C83 describe the methodological contribution. The analytical solutions (Equations 3-5) and phase diagrams (Figures 4-5) demonstrate systematic exploration of parameter space, addressing the limitation of prior numerical approaches (C81) that could not systematically explore all dynamical regimes.

result: Transitions between contraction and extension could help understand in vivo oscillatory behaviors and actomyosin waves. Oscillations might arise through Hopf bifurcation in the multiple-solution regime. The mechanisms could apply to higher-dimensional assemblies and stress fiber formation, and could serve as guiding principles for understanding cytoskeletal self-organization.
evaluation: Claims C101, C102, C103, C105, and C106 are speculative statements about future applications and extensions. While supported by appropriate citations to relevant biological phenomena, these remain hypotheses requiring experimental validation or further theoretical development. The Hopf bifurcation speculation (C102) is particularly tentative.

result: Cytoskeletal bundles generate motion in living cells and have structures ranging from organized to disordered. Many non-muscle actomyosin structures and motor-microtubule assemblies are dynamic with continuously assembling and disassembling components. Actomyosin structures are overwhelmingly observed to contract.
evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C8, C9, C10, and C80 establish background knowledge supported by appropriate citations and general scientific knowledge. These provide context for the work but are not novel findings of this manuscript.

result: Existing models predominantly predict disordered structures are contractile, but the mechanisms underlying actomyosin contraction are unclear since individual motors can elicit extension or contraction. Three classes of models have been proposed: mechanical nonlinearities, motor dwelling, and self-organization. Previous studies involved partial treatments of the three dynamical processes, and experimental discrimination between models remains limited.
evaluation: Claims C3, C11-C16, and C20 provide a literature review establishing the scientific context and gap. The assessment is supported by appropriate citations to theoretical models (Dasanayake et al., 2011; Lenz et al., 2012b; Foster et al., 2015; Kruse and Sekimoto, 2002; etc.) and accurately characterizes the state of the field.

result: Similar nonuniform motor distributions have previously been studied to explain length-dependence of microtubule depolymerization rates.
evaluation: Claim C37 acknowledges prior work on nonuniform motor distributions with appropriate citations (Varga et al., 2006; Reese et al., 2011). This contextualizes the depletion mechanism within existing literature.

result: The number of myosins in individual thick filaments is regulated dynamically in smooth muscle. Other mechanisms for contractility based on sarcomere-like crosslinking have been proposed for fission yeast.
evaluation: Claims C60 and C66 cite relevant biological phenomena and alternative mechanisms with appropriate references (Seow, 2005; Thiyagarajan et al., 2017). These provide biological context and acknowledge alternative explanations.

result: A similarly reduced force could arise in bundles densely covered by motors due to delayed alignment of myosin minifilaments with antiparallel actin filaments.
evaluation: Claim C92 is a speculation about an alternative physical mechanism that could produce similar effects. While plausible, this remains an untested hypothesis without supporting evidence or calculations.

result: Positional ordering of filaments within bundles is suppressed by filament diffusion and is not observed in many disordered actomyosin bundles.
evaluation: Claim C104 is supported by appropriate citations to both theoretical work (Zemel and Mogilner, 2009) and experimental observations (Cramer et al., 1997; Kamasaki et al., 2007). This contextualizes the scope of the present model.
